brief: Intro to a post on Postgres indexing pitfalls; covers unused indexes bloating writes; one client had 23 indexes on one table, write throughput doubled after dropping 14.
facts: Client had 23 indexes on one table
Write throughput doubled after dropping 14 indexes
draft:
When it comes to Postgres performance, indexes are often treated as a silver bullet. Need a faster query? Add an index. But here's the thing: every index you add comes with a hidden cost, and over time, those costs can quietly erode your database's write performance.

Unused indexes are one of the most common — and most overlooked — pitfalls. Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain every index on the table, which means indexes that never serve a single query are still bloating your writes, inflating your storage, and slowing down your vacuum cycles.

We saw this firsthand with a recent client. One of their core tables had accumulated 23 indexes over the years. After a careful audit, we dropped 14 of them — and write throughput doubled. No hardware changes, no query rewrites, just less unnecessary work on every write.

In this post, we'll walk through the most common Postgres indexing pitfalls, show you how to identify unused indexes in your own database, and share a practical checklist for keeping your indexes lean. Whether you're running a small side project or a high-traffic production system, there's something here for you. Let's get started.

brief: Engineering postmortem-style post on a 4-hour outage caused by an expired TLS cert on an internal service; 3 action items.
facts: Caused by an expired TLS certificate on an internal service
draft:
On Tuesday, our platform experienced a 4-hour outage that affected a significant portion of our users. The root cause: an expired TLS certificate on an internal service that sat squarely in our request path. We know how disruptive this was, and we're sharing this postmortem in the spirit of transparency — both to explain what happened and to outline what we're changing.

The short version is humbling. A certificate we didn't realize was close to expiry, on a service most of us rarely thought about, expired quietly — and took a surprising amount of our stack down with it. Alerts fired, but the failure mode was confusing, and it took longer than it should have to trace the cascading errors back to their source.

In the sections below, we'll walk through the full timeline, the contributing factors, and the 3 action items we're committing to: automated certificate-expiry monitoring across all services, documented rotation runbooks for every internal certificate, and regular game-day testing of certificate failure modes.

Outages are painful, but they're also our best teachers. We hope that sharing the details openly helps other teams avoid falling into the same trap. Let's dig into what happened.

brief: Engineering lead: finished 9-month migration from monolith to microservices at a fintech; p99 latency down 40%; 3 teams involved.
draft:
After 9 months, 3 teams, and countless whiteboard sessions — we did it.

This week, we officially completed our migration from a monolith to microservices at our fintech.

The results speak for themselves:
📉 p99 latency down 40%
🚀 Deployments that used to take hours now take minutes
🤝 3 teams shipping independently without stepping on each other

But here's what nobody tells you about migrations like this: the technical work is the easy part. The hard part is alignment. Getting 3 teams to agree on service boundaries, ownership, and standards took more energy than any line of code.

My biggest lessons:
1. Start with the domain, not the technology
2. Migrate incrementally — big bangs fail
3. Celebrate small wins along the way

To everyone who says microservices are overhyped: sometimes they're exactly the right tool for the job.

brief: The ROI of documentation: after writing runbooks, on-call pages dropped 30% in one quarter; team of 9 SREs.
draft:
Want to reduce on-call pain? Write things down.

I know — documentation isn't glamorous. Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks. But here's what happened when our team of 9 SREs finally committed to it:

On-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter.

Not because our systems magically got better. Because our knowledge stopped living exclusively in people's heads.

Here's what we did:
📖 Every incident got a runbook entry — no exceptions
🔁 Every repeated page triggered a documentation review
🧹 We deleted outdated docs as aggressively as we wrote new ones
✅ Runbook quality became part of our definition of done

The ROI of documentation is invisible until you measure it. Fewer 2 AM wake-ups. Faster onboarding. Less bus factor. Calmer on-call rotations.

Documentation isn't a chore. It's an investment with compounding returns.

If your team is drowning in pages, don't buy another tool. Write a runbook.

How does your team approach documentation? I'd love to hear what's worked for you. 👇

brief: Founder shares the 5 tools their 12-person team runs on: Linear, Notion, Slack, Figma, and a homegrown deploy bot named "Otto".
draft:
People often ask how our 12-person team stays productive without a big ops function.

The answer? We run the entire company on just 5 tools:

1️⃣ Linear — every task, bug, and project lives here. If it's not in Linear, it doesn't exist.
2️⃣ Notion — our company brain. Docs, wikis, meeting notes, onboarding.
3️⃣ Slack — communication, with strict channel hygiene to keep the noise down.
4️⃣ Figma — where every product idea becomes real before a single line of code is written.
5️⃣ Otto — our homegrown deploy bot. One command, and code goes from PR to production. Everyone's favorite teammate.

That's it. No sprawling tool stack. No overlapping subscriptions. No "wait, which doc is the source of truth?"

The principle behind it: every new tool adds a tax. Context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations. We only add a tool when the pain of not having it exceeds that tax.

Simplicity is a competitive advantage.

brief: Executive summary of a data-governance whitepaper: survey of 156 enterprises; 44% have no data-classification policy; recommends 5-step maturity model.
draft:
Data has become every enterprise's most valuable asset — and, increasingly, its most significant liability. To understand how organizations are managing this tension, we surveyed 156 enterprises across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities.

The findings reveal a substantial maturity gap. Most notably, 44% of surveyed enterprises have no data-classification policy in place, leaving them unable to consistently identify which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical. Without classification as a foundation, downstream controls — access management, retention, encryption, and incident response — rest on guesswork rather than policy.

The consequences are not hypothetical. Organizations lacking foundational governance report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and mounting friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close the gap, this whitepaper recommends a practical 5-step maturity model that guides organizations from initial data discovery through classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring. Each step includes concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria to help teams benchmark progress.

Data governance is no longer a back-office concern — it is a prerequisite for compliance, security, and AI readiness. The organizations that act now will be positioned to move faster, and more safely, than those that wait.

brief: Thread: opener + 4 tweets summarizing a paper finding LLM judges agree with humans 81% of the time but drop to 64% on creative tasks.
facts: LLM judges agree with humans 81% of the time
Agreement drops to 64% on creative tasks
draft:
Can LLMs judge other LLMs?

A new paper puts "LLM-as-judge" to the test — and the results are a wake-up call for anyone using AI to evaluate AI.

The key findings, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ The headline: LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time overall. That's genuinely impressive — for many routine evaluation tasks, an LLM judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ But here's the catch: on creative tasks, agreement drops to 64%. When there's no objectively "correct" answer — style, originality, taste — LLM judges and humans part ways dramatically.

3/ Why the gap? One likely culprit: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length over genuine creativity. In other words, LLM judges like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ Takeaway: LLM-as-judge is a powerful tool, not a replacement. Use it for scale on objective tasks — but for creative work, keep humans in the loop. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.
